case.title: UNIPARK smishing infrastructure
case.boundary: Exact artefact matches support a shared phishing-kit family. They do not prove that one operator controlled every hostname, identify the SMS sender, reveal a private administration panel or count successful victims.

nodes.label: Received UNIPARK-themed SMS
nodes.meaning: The supplied screenshot preserved the sender, delivery time, payment lure and defanged destination used as the investigation seed.

nodes.label: unipark.fmqr[.]ink/com
nodes.meaning: The SMS destination used a newly registered root domain, a brand subdomain and the /com route. It already resolved to the NKSC sinkhole during collection.

nodes.label: Captured frontend bundles
nodes.meaning: Static collection preserved the brand layer, shared application engine, Socket.IO client and anti-analysis logic without executing the page.

nodes.label: Same-origin /console channel
nodes.meaning: The frontend constructs a same-origin Socket.IO connection at /console and exposes bidirectional state events. The path is not a unique IOC or a proven public admin panel.

nodes.label: Exact-hash kit linkage
nodes.meaning: Four exact JS/CSS hashes linked the supplied deployment to an earlier UNIPARK host. A shared core-bundle hash expanded the pivot to 163 public scans.

nodes.label: 126 unique related hostnames
nodes.meaning: Deduplicating page hostnames across 163 exact-core-hash URLScan records produced 126 hosts spanning several parking brands. This is not a victim count.

nodes.label: Reusable operator-driven payment kit
nodes.meaning: The shared engine, configurable brand layer, payment flow and server-directed screens support a high-confidence reusable phishing-kit assessment.

nodes.label: Operator and complete backend unknown
nodes.meaning: Public scans cannot reveal private hosts, hidden origins, server-side relays or a separate dashboard. Shared code can be sold, rented or copied, so kit lineage is not operator attribution.
